claim: Neurons in navigational brain regions provide information about position, orientation, and speed relative to environmental landmarks.
source: Neurons in navigational brain regions provide information about position, orientation, and speed relative to environmental landmarks.
evidence: This is a general statement about navigational neurons supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Neurons in navigational brain regions change their firing patterns ('remap') in response to changing contextual factors such as environmental cues, task conditions, and behavioral states.
source: These cells also change their firing patterns ('remap') in response to changing contextual factors such as environmental cues, task conditions, and behavioral states, which influence neural activity throughout the brain.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations throughout the manuscript and represents established knowledge about remapping in navigational circuits.

claim: RNN models trained on combined navigation and context inference tasks produce activity patterns qualitatively similar to population-wide remapping in the entorhinal cortex.
source: We show that these combined task constraints (navigation and context inference) produce activity patterns that are qualitatively similar to population-wide remapping in the entorhinal cortex, a navigational brain region.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from RNN models shown in Figure 1.

claim: The RNN models identify a solution that generalizes to more complex navigation and inference tasks.
source: Furthermore, the models identify a solution that generalizes to more complex navigation and inference tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing the models work in 2D environments (Figure 4) and with multiple maps (Figure 5).

claim: Neural circuit computations throughout the brain are shaped by combinations of internal and external factors.
source: Neural circuit computations throughout the brain, from the primary sensory cortex (Bennett et al., 2013; Niell and Stryker, 2010; Vinck et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2014) to higher cognitive areas, (Boccara et al., 2019; Butler et al., 2019; Hardcastle et al., 2017b; Hulse et al., 2017; Pettit et al., 2022) are shaped by combinations of internal and external factors.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Internal state changes such as shifts in attention, thirst, arousal, and impulsivity can profoundly alter neural activity across multiple brain areas.
source: Internal state changes, such as shifts in attention (Fenton et al., 2010; Kentros et al., 2004; Pettit et al., 2022), thirst (Allen et al., 2019), arousal (Stringer et al., 2019), and impulsivity (Cowley et al., 2020), can profoundly alter neural activity across multiple brain areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Neurons in the medial entorhinal cortex typically represent one or more features such as spatial position, heading direction, and environmental landmarks.
source: For example, neurons in the medial entorhinal cortex typically represent one or more features such as spatial position, heading direction, and environmental landmarks and are therefore thought to support navigation (Diehl et al., 2017; Gil et al., 2018; Hafting et al., 2005; Hardcastle et al., 2017a; Høydal et al., 2019; Moser et al., 2014; Sargolini et al., 2006; Solstad et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Entorhinal cortex neurons are thought to support navigation.
source: For example, neurons in the medial entorhinal cortex typically represent one or more features such as spatial position, heading direction, and environmental landmarks and are therefore thought to support navigation (Diehl et al., 2017; Gil et al., 2018; Hafting et al., 2005; Hardcastle et al., 2017a; Høydal et al., 2019; Moser et al., 2014; Sargolini et al., 2006; Solstad et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and represents an inference from the observed neural representations.

claim: Entorhinal cortex neurons change their firing rates and shift their spatial firing positions ('remap') under a variety of circumstances, even when navigational cues remain stable.
source: At the same time, these neurons change their firing rates and shift their spatial firing positions—or 'remap'—under a variety of circumstances, even when navigational cues remain stable (Bant et al., 2020; Boccara et al., 2019; Butler et al., 2019; Campbell et al., 2021; Campbell et al., 2018; Hardcastle et al., 2017b; Low et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Theoretical models propose that remapping occurs because cells are responding to global contextual cues in order to decorrelate related experiences with distinct contextual relevance.
source: Theoretical models of this phenomenon propose that remapping occurs because these cells are responding to global contextual cues (like arousal or attention) in order to decorrelate related experiences with distinct contextual relevance (Colgin et al., 2008; Sanders et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: Remapping could enable animals to form distinct memories or choose appropriate actions for a given set of circumstances.
source: This process could enable animals to form distinct memories or choose appropriate actions for a given set of circumstances.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential function of remapping.

claim: Existing normative models of remapping do not address how a biological system might implement this strategy.
source: However, these normative models (i.e. theories for why remapping occurs; Levenstein et al., 2020) do not address how a biological system might implement this strategy.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of existing models based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Low et al. (2021) demonstrated that remapping in the medial entorhinal cortex simultaneously recruited large populations of neurons across the entorhinal cortical circuit.
source: In this study, Low et al. demonstrated that remapping in the medial entorhinal cortex simultaneously recruited large populations of neurons across the entorhinal cortical circuit.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Low et al., 2021.

claim: Remapping in Low et al. (2021) comprised discrete transitions between aligned neural activity manifolds, which each represented a distinct map of an unchanging, virtual reality 1D environment.
source: Remapping comprised discrete transitions between aligned neural activity manifolds, which each represented a distinct map of an unchanging, virtual reality 1D environment (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Low et al., 2021 and reference to Figure 1C-D.

claim: Remapping in Low et al. (2021) was not aligned to particular track positions, rewards, or landmarks.
source: Remapping was not aligned to particular track positions, rewards, or landmarks.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Low et al., 2021.

claim: Remapping in Low et al. (2021) correlated with transient decreases in running speed.
source: Instead, remapping correlated with transient decreases in running speed (Figure 1B), which could correspond to discrete changes in a latent state (such as shifts in arousal, task engagement, or other behavioral states).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Low et al., 2021 and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Transient decreases in running speed could correspond to discrete changes in a latent state such as shifts in arousal, task engagement, or other behavioral states.
source: Instead, remapping correlated with transient decreases in running speed (Figure 1B), which could correspond to discrete changes in a latent state (such as shifts in arousal, task engagement, or other behavioral states).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about what the running speed changes might represent.

claim: Trained RNNs achieve 100% correct state estimation.
source: Trained RNNs achieve high performance in both tasks, indicating that they can correctly form a persistent representation of each latent state while maintaining a stable position estimate across states (100% correct state estimation; average angular position error after 300 steps, mean ± standard deviation: 8.13° ± 0.51°; Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the trained RNN models.

claim: Trained RNNs achieve an average angular position error after 300 steps of 8.13° ± 0.51°.
source: Trained RNNs achieve high performance in both tasks, indicating that they can correctly form a persistent representation of each latent state while maintaining a stable position estimate across states (100% correct state estimation; average angular position error after 300 steps, mean ± standard deviation: 8.13° ± 0.51°; Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the trained RNN models.

claim: Single RNN units and network-wide activity alternated between distinct maps of the same environment across the two latent states.
source: As in biological data (Figure 1C), single units and network-wide activity alternated between distinct maps of the same environment across the two latent states (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Single RNN units remapped heterogeneously.
source: Similar to biological neurons, single RNN units remapped heterogeneously (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNN units changed their spatial firing field locations to a similar extent as biological neurons.
source: Units changed their spatial firing field locations to a similar extent as biological neurons, but changes in firing rate were more common in the model units.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changes in firing rate were more common in the model units than in biological neurons.
source: Units changed their spatial firing field locations to a similar extent as biological neurons, but changes in firing rate were more common in the model units.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When projected into the subspace defined by the first three principal components, RNN activity occupied two distinct rings, where position along each ring corresponded to position on the linear track.
source: When we projected the hidden layer activity into the subspace defined by the first three principle components, the activity occupied two distinct rings, where position along each ring corresponded to position on the linear track (Figure 1H, red to blue color map).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The top three principal components explained ~50% of the variance in RNN activity.
source: Together, these top three components explained ~50% of the variance (Figure 1I, red points).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The ring manifolds in RNN models were more aligned in high-dimensional activity space than expected by chance for all trained models.
source: As in Low et al., 2021, we used Procrustes shape analysis to demonstrate that these rings were more aligned in high-dimensional activity space than expected by chance for all trained models, such that the position along one ring matched the position on the second ring (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1J using Procrustes analysis.

claim: The position along one ring matched the position on the second ring in RNN models.
source: As in Low et al., 2021, we used Procrustes shape analysis to demonstrate that these rings were more aligned in high-dimensional activity space than expected by chance for all trained models, such that the position along one ring matched the position on the second ring (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The combined task constraints of navigation and context inference are sufficient to organize randomly initialized synaptic weights into a network model that qualitatively reproduces the remapping dynamics and representational geometry observed in the entorhinal cortex.
source: Thus, these task constraints are sufficient to organize randomly initialized synaptic weights into a network model that qualitatively reproduces the remapping dynamics and representational geometry that Low et al., 2021 observed in the entorhinal cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNN modeling results presented in Figure 1.

claim: The RNN must maintain an estimate of a 1D circular position, which is best achieved through approximate ring attractors.
source: First, the RNN must maintain an estimate of a 1D circular position, which is best achieved through approximate ring attractors (Cueva et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and represents established knowledge about ring attractors.

claim: The RNN model forms two ring attractors, one for each of the two distinct latent state conditions.
source: Thus, we expect the model to form two ring attractors, one for each of the two distinct latent state conditions.
evidence: This is an inference about what the model should do based on the task design.

claim: The network should develop separate orthogonal subspaces for position and latent state because it must track two statistically independent information streams.
source: Second, the network must track two statistically independent information streams and should, therefore, develop separate orthogonal subspaces for each stream (Kaufman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and represents an inference about how the network should organize information.

claim: The position subspace contains the position tuning curves for all neurons, as well as the RNN readout weights for the position.
source: One subspace, the 'position subspace,' should contain the position tuning curves for all neurons, as well as the RNN readout weights for the position.
evidence: This is a definition of the position subspace based on the task design.

claim: The remapping dimension is tuned to changes in the latent state and contains the readout weights for the state.
source: The other subspace, the 'remapping dimension,' should be tuned to changes in the latent state and contain the readout weights for the state.
evidence: This is a definition of the remapping dimension based on the task design.

claim: The position subspace and remapping dimension are orthogonal to one another in RNN models.
source: We confirmed that these dimensions were orthogonal to one another (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Methods), such that changes in the latent state do not interfere with changes in position and vice versa.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Changes in the latent state do not interfere with changes in position and vice versa in RNN models.
source: We confirmed that these dimensions were orthogonal to one another (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Methods), such that changes in the latent state do not interfere with changes in position and vice versa.
evidence: This is an inference from the orthogonality of the subspaces.

claim: The task does not require the two-ring manifolds to be strictly aligned in high-dimensional activity space.
source: However, as we show in detail below, the task does not require the two-ring manifolds to be strictly aligned in high-dimensional activity space.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim demonstrated through mathematical analysis in the manuscript.

claim: The RNN maintains a stable position estimate in spite of switches in the latent state that may occur anywhere along the circular track.
source: The RNN maintains a stable position estimate in spite of switches in the latent state—which we call 'remapping events'—that may occur anywhere along the circular track.
evidence: This is a description of the RNN behavior based on the task design.

claim: The RNN must implement an invertible remapping function to match track locations across the two ring manifolds.
source: To do so, the RNN must implement an invertible remapping function to match track locations across the two ring manifolds.
evidence: This is an inference about what the RNN must do to maintain stable position estimates across remapping events.

claim: A complex remapping function implemented using recurrent dynamics could lead to a delay between the latent state signal and remapping.
source: The RNN could implement a complex remapping function using its recurrent dynamics, but this implementation could lead to a delay between the latent state signal and remapping.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential consequences of different implementation strategies.

claim: The RNN converges to a simpler configuration that allows the linear input layer to implement remapping, enabling rapid remapping in a single timestep.
source: We therefore reasoned that the RNN might converge to the simpler configuration, allowing the linear input layer to implement remapping and thereby enabling rapid remapping in a single timestep.
evidence: This is an inference about why the RNN might adopt a particular solution strategy.

claim: RNN models trained on a simultaneous latent state inference and navigation task converge to a geometrically simple solution out of the space of all possible, high-dimensional solutions.
source: Altogether, these findings suggest that RNN models trained on a simultaneous latent state inference and navigation task converge to a geometrically simple solution out of the space of all possible, high-dimensional solutions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the geometric analysis of the RNN models.

claim: The simpler RNN solution recapitulates the geometry of entorhinal cortical dynamics during remapping in virtual reality environments.
source: This simpler solution recapitulates the geometry of entorhinal cortical dynamics during remapping in virtual reality environments (Low et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to data from Low et al., 2021.

claim: Neither the RNN nor the biological data are consistent with the simplest 3-dimensional solution.
source: Notably, neither the RNN nor the biological data are consistent with the simplest 3-dimensional solution, as evidenced by the imperfect ring alignment (Low et al., 2021 and Figure 1J), the variable remapping vectors (Figure 2C–D), and the dimensionality of the network dynamics (which is >3; Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in multiple figures and comparison to biological data.

claim: Approximately 60% of fixed points in the trained RNN were located on one of the two ring manifolds and largely had marginally stable linear dynamics.
source: Roughly 60% of these fixed points were located on one of the two previously described ring manifolds and largely had marginally stable linear dynamics (largest Jacobian eigenvalue ≈1; Figure 3, color-coded green).
evidence: This claim is supported by fixed point analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The remaining fixed points in the trained RNN were located between the two ring manifolds and had unstable dynamics.
source: The remaining fixed points were located between the two ring manifolds and had unstable dynamics (largest Jacobian eigenvalue >1; Figure 3, color-coded gold).
evidence: This claim is supported by fixed point analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The RNN dynamics implement a pair of ring attractors.
source: In essence, this analysis confirms that the RNN dynamics indeed implemented a pair of ring attractors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fixed point analysis.

claim: A collection of unstable fixed points form a boundary between the two stable ring attractor basins.
source: Furthermore, a collection of unstable fixed points form a boundary between the two stable ring attractor basins.
evidence: This is an inference from the fixed point analysis.

claim: The intermediate fixed points are unstable along a small number of dimensions (i.e. saddle fixed points) which 'funnel' neural activity to the appropriate location during a remapping event.
source: In line with observations by Sussillo and Barak, 2013 on a discrete flip-flop task, these intermediate fixed points are unstable along a small number of dimensions (i.e. saddle fixed points; Figure 3D, gold points) which 'funnel' neural activity to the appropriate location during a remapping event.
evidence: This claim is supported by fixed point analysis data shown in Figure 3D and comparison to prior work.

claim: For fixed points along the two ring attractors, the principal eigenvector corresponds to a slow dimension along which activity does not grow or decay.
source: For the fixed points along the two ring attractors, this eigenvector corresponds to a slow dimension along which x does not grow or decay (i.e. its associated eigenvalue λ≈1; Figure 3D, green points).
evidence: This claim is supported by eigenvector analysis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The principal eigenvectors for fixed points along the ring attractors were nearly orthogonal to the remapping dimension and aligned with the position subspace.
source: Consistent with a mechanism for integrating positional information, these eigenvectors were nearly orthogonal to the remapping dimension and aligned with the position subspace (Figure 3E–G, green).
evidence: This claim is supported by eigenvector analysis data shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: For unstable fixed points, the principal eigenvector corresponds to a dimension along which activity moves rapidly away from the fixed point.
source: Conversely, for the unstable fixed points, the principal eigenvector corresponds to a dimension along which x moves rapidly away from the fixed point (i.e. its associated eigenvalue λ>1; Figure 3D, gold points).
evidence: This claim is supported by eigenvector analysis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The principal eigenvectors for unstable fixed points were aligned with the remapping dimension and nearly orthogonal to the position subspace.
source: Consistent with a mechanism for 'funneling' activity during remapping events, these eigenvectors were aligned with the remapping dimension and nearly orthogonal to the position subspace (Figure 3E–F, yellow).
evidence: This claim is supported by eigenvector analysis data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: RNN models trained on 2D navigation with latent state inference performed well on both components of the task.
source: As before, the models performed well on both components of the task (mean loss ± sem: position estimate, 0.036 ± 1.1 × 10–3; latent state estimate, 0.002 ± 1.9 × 10–5; n = 15 models) (Figure 4A), and single unit activity was modulated by both spatial position and latent state (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by performance data for 2D navigation models.

claim: In 2D navigation RNN models, activity occupied two distinct toroidal manifolds with the position on each torus corresponding to the position in the 2D space.
source: When we projected the activity into a subspace defined by the first three principal components, the activity occupied two distinct toroidal manifolds with the position on each torus corresponding to the position in the 2D space (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Four principal components explained ~50% of the variance in network activity for 2D navigation RNN models.
source: In keeping with these qualitative observations, four principal components explained ~50% of the variance in network activity (Figure 4D), and the manifolds were again highly, though not perfectly, aligned in the full-dimensional activity space (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The toroidal manifolds in 2D navigation RNN models were highly, though not perfectly, aligned in the full-dimensional activity space.
source: In keeping with these qualitative observations, four principal components explained ~50% of the variance in network activity (Figure 4D), and the manifolds were again highly, though not perfectly, aligned in the full-dimensional activity space (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: By holding either the horizontal or vertical position variable constant during the RNN simulation, a pair of 1D-aligned ring manifolds can be recovered from the 2D toroidal manifolds.
source: By holding either the horizontal (X) or vertical (Y) position variable constant during the RNN simulation, we recover a pair of 1D-aligned ring manifolds (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The geometry of the original 1D task can be recovered by taking 'slices' through the toroidal manifolds in 2D navigation models.
source: That is, we can recover the geometry of the original 1D task (see Figure 1) by taking 'slices' through the toroidal manifolds.
evidence: This is an inference from the data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The remapping and position dimensions were orthogonalized in 2D navigation RNN models.
source: The remapping and position dimensions were again orthogonalized in these models (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Models trained on a 2D navigation task with latent state inference identified a geometrically similar solution to those trained on a 1D task.
source: Thus models trained on a 2D navigation task with latent state inference identified a geometrically similar solution to those trained on a 1D task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparison of 1D and 2D model results.

claim: Spontaneous remapping is possible in 2D and may operate under similar mechanisms as in 1D.
source: These findings demonstrate that spontaneous remapping is possible in 2D and may operate under similar mechanisms as in 1D.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the 2D modeling results.

claim: RNN models trained to navigate in 1D while tracking three binary state switch cues performed well on both task components.
source: Models performed well on both task components (mean loss ± sem: position estimate, 0.013 ± 3.6 × 10–4; latent state estimate, 0.0039 ± 4.9 × 10–5; n=15 models) and single unit activity was modulated by both spatial position and latent state (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by performance data for 3-map models.

claim: The essential geometry of the original task was preserved in 3-map RNN models.
source: Importantly, we found that the same essential geometry of the original task was preserved.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from analysis of 3-map models.

claim: Ring manifolds in 3-map RNN models were qualitatively aligned when visualized using PCA.
source: When we visualized each pair of maps using PCA, the ring manifolds were again qualitatively aligned (Figure 5C, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The three maps in 3-map RNN models were organized as vertices of an equilateral triangle when projected into the same subspace.
source: Projecting the activity from all three maps into the same subspace revealed that they were further organized as vertices of an equilateral triangle (Figure 5C, left)—i.e., the acute angle between any two remapping dimensions was 60° (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The acute angle between any two remapping dimensions in 3-map RNN models was 60°.
source: Projecting the activity from all three maps into the same subspace revealed that they were further organized as vertices of an equilateral triangle (Figure 5C, left)—i.e., the acute angle between any two remapping dimensions was 60° (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The network geometry in 3-map RNN models was relatively low-dimensional, with 4 principal components explaining ~60% of the variance and 14 principal components explaining ~90% of the variance.
source: Again, the network geometry was relatively low-dimensional (4 principal components explained ~60% of the variance; 14 principal components,~90% of the variance)(Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: All pairs of manifolds in 3-map RNN models were highly aligned relative to chance, with a similar degree of alignment across ring manifold pairs and across RNNs.
source: Procrustes analysis revealed that all pairs of manifolds were highly aligned relative to chance, with a similar degree of alignment across ring manifold pairs and across RNNs (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Positional and latent state information were orthogonalized in 3-map RNN models.
source: Finally, positional and latent state information were orthogonalized, as before (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: RNNs are capable of solving the navigation and latent state inference task with larger numbers of latent states (more than three, up to 10 states).
source: In Figure 5—figure supplement 1, we show that RNNs are capable of solving this task with larger numbers of latent states (more than three; for simplicity, we consider up to 10 states).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The RNN dynamics and geometry generalize to larger numbers of latent states: each latent state is associated with a different ring attractor and every pair of ring attractors is highly aligned.
source: Furthermore, the RNN dynamics and geometry generalize accordingly: each latent state is associated with a different ring attractor and every pair of ring attractors is highly aligned.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from analysis of models with varying numbers of latent states.

claim: Low et al. (2021) observed remapping between 3-4 stable maps of the same virtual track in a subset of experimental sessions (N=4 sessions from 2 mice).
source: Motivated by these observations, we revisited a subset of experimental sessions from Low et al., 2021 (N=4 sessions from 2 mice) that exhibited remapping between 3–4 stable maps of the same virtual track (Figure 6A, B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1) for a pilot comparison with the RNN models, which we hope will inspire future experimental analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Low et al., 2021 and reference to Figure 6.

claim: Remapping events in multi-map sessions from Low et al. (2021) did not reflect recording probe movement, as confirmed by comparing waveforms from different maps across the session, which were highly stable.
source: As Low et al., we first confirmed that these remapping events did not reflect recording probe movement by comparing the waveforms from different maps across the session, which were highly stable (Figure 6B, right; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by waveform analysis data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In many multi-map sessions from Low et al. (2021), population-wide activity across pairs of maps occupied distinct, qualitatively aligned rings, where the position along each ring corresponded to the position along the virtual track.
source: To examine the manifold structure of the neural data, we projected the neural tuning curves associated with each pair of maps into the subspace defined by the first three principle components. In many sessions, population-wide activity across the two maps occupied distinct, qualitatively aligned rings, where the position along each ring corresponded to the position along the virtual track (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Pairs of maps in multi-map sessions from Low et al. (2021) were largely more aligned than expected by chance (13/18 map pairs more aligned than shuffle).
source: Procrustes analysis revealed that these pairs of maps were largely more aligned than expected by chance (Figure 6D; 13/18 map pairs more aligned than shuffle).
evidence: This claim is supported by Procrustes analysis data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Five map pairs from one mouse in the Low et al. (2021) multi-map sessions were not aligned, suggesting that manifold alignment does not always emerge in biological data.
source: Notably, five map pairs from one mouse (three in session A, two in session D) were not aligned (Figure 6D, black and teal points), suggesting that manifold alignment does not always emerge in biological data.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D and represents an inference about biological variability.

claim: There was a range of acute angles between pairs of remapping dimensions in biological multi-map sessions, suggesting more asymmetry in the biological network geometry than in the model.
source: Finally, we asked whether the remapping dimensions from the biological sessions were organized symmetrically, as in the model (Figure 6E, left). We found that there was a range of acute angles between pairs of remapping dimensions (Figure 6E, right), suggesting that there was more asymmetry in the biological network geometry than in the model.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and comparison to model predictions.

claim: RNNs initialized from random synaptic weights recapitulate the essential features of biological data—aligned ring manifolds—when trained to remember a binary latent state variable and to simultaneously integrate a velocity signal in a circular environment.
source: Here, we used RNN models to explore a normative hypothesis that these remapping dynamics reflect hidden state inference (Colgin et al., 2008; Sanders et al., 2020). We showed that RNNs initialized from random synaptic weights recapitulate the essential features of biological data—aligned ring manifolds (Low et al., 2021)—when trained to remember a binary latent state variable and to simultaneously integrate a velocity signal in a circular environment.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: RNNs learn to represent positional and state change information in orthogonal subspaces such that navigation and latent state inference co-occur without interference.
source: RNNs learn to represent positional and state change information in orthogonal subspaces such that navigation and latent state inference co-occur without interference.
evidence: This is a summary finding supported by data in Figures 1, 4, and 5.

claim: The geometry and algorithmic principles of the RNN solution readily generalize to more complex tasks including navigation in 2D environments and tasks involving three or more latent states.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that the geometry and algorithmic principles of this solution readily generalize to more complex tasks including navigation in 2D environments and tasks involving three or more latent states.
evidence: This is a summary finding supported by data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Fenton et al. (2010) proposed that the hippocampus constructs multiple spatial maps that are anchored to different landmarks, and when the animal's attention switches between these reference points, hippocampal cells remap.
source: Fenton et al., 2010 proposed that the hippocampus constructs multiple spatial maps that are anchored to different landmarks; when the animal's attention switches between these reference points, hippocampal cells remap (see also Kubie et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The hippocampal circuit groups navigational episodes into discrete categories by combining internal context with external landmarks.
source: This proposal is consistent with the idea that the hippocampal circuit groups navigational episodes into discrete categories by combining internal context with external landmarks (Colgin et al., 2008; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2007; Sanders et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: An animal's prior experience with an environment can shape how the hippocampus delineates categories of navigational episodes.
source: Related experimental work demonstrates that an animal's prior experience with an environment can shape how the hippocampus delineates these categories (Plitt and Giocomo, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Sheintuch et al. (2020) reported similar experimental findings to Low et al. (2021) in the hippocampus, highlighting the broad relevance of the remapping phenomenon.
source: While we draw explicit comparisons with spontaneous remapping in the entorhinal cortex (Low et al., 2021), Sheintuch et al., 2020 reported similar experimental findings in the hippocampus, highlighting the broad relevance of this remapping phenomenon and our modeling efforts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Low et al. (2021) found that remapping was correlated with brief decreases in running speed.
source: Indeed, Low et al. found that remapping was correlated with brief decreases in running speed (Low et al., 2021), suggesting that this temporary behavioral state change—which is known to have widespread impacts on global brain activity (Stringer et al., 2019)—may serve as an external trigger of remapping in the entorhinal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Low et al., 2021.

claim: Brief decreases in running speed are known to have widespread impacts on global brain activity.
